title: Agent Permissions Best Practices
summary: Least privilege, action-level scopes, user-aware permissions, approvals for high-risk actions, and reviews — treating permissions as dynamic controls.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**The permission that causes the incident is rarely the one anyone approved on purpose. It's the one nobody took back.** Agents don't usually lose access over time. They accumulate it: a scope added for a one-off task, a broad role attached because enumerating actions was slower, a credential nobody remembered to pull when the project wrapped.


Most teams treat permissions as a setup field. Configure the agent once, grant enough scope to avoid friction, move on. Six months later, nobody can say with confidence what that agent can actually do.


Granting broadly "just in case" feels efficient and isn't. Every capability an agent holds but doesn't use is still part of its blast radius the day something goes wrong, whether that's a manipulated prompt, a buggy tool call, or a model that reasons its way somewhere nobody intended.


We think the fix isn't one control. It's treating each grant as something that has to keep earning its place: narrow at first, scoped to a specific action, checked against the user the agent is acting for, and pulled back the moment it stops being justified.


Start with the agent nobody has looked at since it shipped. That's usually where the gap is.


## Overview


Agent permissions define two things: what an agent can reach, and what it's allowed to do once it gets there. As agents connect to CRMs, data warehouses, ticketing tools, and payment processors, that second question is where most of the risk actually lives.


How authorization gets checked at the moment of the request, the layers, the rule that keeps an agent's effective access from ever exceeding the user it's acting for, is its own subject. What follows here are the practices that keep a permission set worth trusting in the first place, independent of how your stack enforces them.


Six of them carry the weight. Grant narrowly. Scope by action, not by tool. Evaluate every request against the person the agent is acting for. Keep environments apart. Review on a cadence. Remove access cleanly the moment an agent retires. We don't think any of these is exotic on its own. Skipping any one of them is how an agent ends up holding access nobody can explain.


**The shift that matters:** permissions are not a setup field you fill in once. They're a control that has to keep being true.


## Least Privilege


Least privilege is the foundation, and it's simple to state and constantly skipped in practice: an agent should get only the permissions its specific workflow requires, nothing held in reserve.


Take a marketing analytics agent that produces a weekly campaign digest. Its job is to read engagement metrics and post a summary into a channel. It needs read access to the analytics tables and the ability to post to that channel. It does not need to edit the underlying dashboards, adjust ad spend, or export the customer email list. Every capability it lacks is an incident that simply cannot happen to it.


Start from the workflow, not the system. Ask what concrete steps the agent performs, grant exactly those, and resist rounding up to a broader role because it's faster to configure.


**Rule of thumb:** if you can't name the workflow step that justifies a permission, the agent doesn't get it.


## Action-Level Scopes


Connecting an agent to a system is not the same as letting it do everything that system supports. Inside a single tool, distinct actions carry very different risk:


- **Read:** view a record, query a table, fetch a document
- **Write:** create or update a record
- **Delete:** remove data, often irreversibly
- **Export:** move data out of the system entirely
- **Send:** dispatch a message to an internal or external recipient
- **Share:** grant access to someone else


Take an expense-report agent connected to the finance system. Reading policy limits and drafting a reimbursement request is reasonable. Letting it post that reimbursement straight to payroll is a different grant entirely, and the two shouldn't share a scope just because they touch the same tool.


Action-level scoping is what makes least privilege enforceable rather than aspirational. "Access to the finance system" is not a control. "Read policy limits, draft reimbursements" is. And for the handful of actions that are genuinely hard to undo, a send that already left the building, a delete with no recycle bin, worth adding one more constraint: whoever configures the agent should be able to say, in a sentence, what happens if this specific action is wrong, and whether that's a decision the agent should be making alone.


## User-Aware Permissions


When an agent acts on behalf of a person, its effective permissions are the intersection of what the agent can do and what that person can do. Never the union. An agent that simply returns whatever it can reach quietly becomes a side door around access controls that already exist.


Take an HR assistant that answers questions about compensation. A team lead asking about their direct reports should get an answer. An individual contributor asking about a colleague's salary should not get the agent's answer, they should get the answer *that specific requester* is entitled to, which in this case is nothing. If the agent only checked its own access, every employee would inherit whatever the service account could see.


` effective_access = agent_permissions ∩ requesting_user_permissions`


This one rule is worth more than most of the others combined, because it's the difference between an agent that respects access controls and one that quietly bypasses them for anyone who knows how to ask.


## Environment Separation


Agents in development shouldn't carry the same permissions as agents in production. Experimental agents change fast, run logic nobody has stress-tested yet, and get built under time pressure, which makes them exactly the wrong candidate for live systems and sensitive data.


A team prototyping an agent that joins customer and revenue tables should work against masked or synthetic data with read-only access while it's still finding its footing. Promotion to production is the moment to attach real credentials and the action-level scopes the workflow actually needs, under review, not by default because the prototype happened to work.


Treating environment as a boundary keeps a half-finished experiment from touching what your customers depend on, and it gives builders room to iterate without production-grade friction slowing down every test run.


## Periodic Reviews


Permissions aren't granted forever, even when nobody explicitly revokes them. Workflows change, integrations get retired, and access that was essential six months ago can sit there as dead weight that only widens the surface an attacker has to work with.


A recurring review puts the burden of justification on the agent's owner. On a fixed cadence, quarterly is common, the owner confirms each permission is still needed, still scoped correctly, and still tied to a workflow that's actually running. Anything that can't be justified gets pulled.


The useful version of this review is a short summary, not a wall of raw grants: this agent holds these scopes, last used them on this date, was last reviewed then. A contract-review agent still holding an export scope it hasn't touched in a quarter becomes an obvious call the moment that history is visible, instead of one more line in a spreadsheet nobody reads.


## Revocation at Offboarding


When an agent retires, its permissions come off immediately, not eventually, not whenever someone remembers. A decommissioned agent that still holds live credentials is one of the more dangerous things sitting in an enterprise, because it's an access path nobody is watching anymore.


Revocation has to be a defined, checkable step in retirement, not a status flag. Deactivate the agent's identity, rotate or invalidate its credentials, and confirm the grants are actually gone in every system it touched. A registry that says "inactive" while the underlying token still works has not revoked anything.


A sales-forecasting agent replaced by a newer version shouldn't leave its old warehouse credentials sitting there, valid and unused. Clean revocation is what keeps a retired agent from becoming a silent door back into systems nobody's watching anymore.


## Avoiding Permission Creep


Every practice above defends against the same slow failure. An agent starts narrow and well-justified. A new feature needs one more scope. A workaround grants temporary access that never gets withdrawn. A broad role gets attached because it's faster than enumerating actions one by one. None of these decisions looks reckless in the moment. The agent that results from all of them together usually is.


**Figure 1 — Without a scheduled review, an unused permission's default state is staying, not going.**


That's why the controls have to be structural instead of aspirational. Least privilege keeps the starting point narrow. Action-level scopes stop a single grant from quietly carrying a high-risk capability. Periodic reviews catch accumulation before it compounds. Revocation at offboarding stops a dead agent from leaving access behind it. Together they turn permissions from a form filled in once into something that stays aligned with what the agent actually does, on an ongoing basis.


## Conclusion


We think strong permission governance is less about telling agents no and more about making sure each one can do its job and nothing more, and that this stays true as the agent, its workflows, and the systems around it keep changing.


Grant narrowly, scope by action, check every request against the user the agent is acting for, keep environments apart, review on a cadence, and revoke cleanly when an agent retires. Each of these is simple on its own. Applied together, they're what keeps autonomy useful instead of letting it quietly turn into power nobody signed off on.


**The agents worth trusting aren't the ones with the fewest permissions. They're the ones whose access you can still account for a year from now.**
